items.prompt: One business event must be processed independently by billing, analytics, and email services, each with its own retry pace. Which pattern fits?
constraints: Consumers must not block one another.
Each consumer needs independent retry and retention.
The producer publishes one logical event.

options.text: Publish the event to an SNS topic and subscribe a separate SQS queue for each consumer so each service receives and retries its own copy.
Send the event directly to one consumer queue and require the consumers to share a single polling process.
Use one Lambda invocation because Lambda automatically retries each subscriber independently without separate event destinations.
Use a security group because network fan-out sends one packet to every consumer service.

feedback.Reason: SNS fan-out with one SQS subscription per consumer separates delivery, retry, backlog, and failure ownership.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: SNS publishes to a topic and delivers a message to each matching subscription. SQS queues buffer and independently retain messages for their consumers.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner configures one queue per bounded context, monitors subscription delivery and queue age, and keeps consumers idempotent.
Details.errorCorrection: A single consumer queue does not provide independent copies, one Lambda path does not automatically create arbitrary subscribers, and security groups do not fan out events.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Fan-out adds queues and policies but prevents a slow or failed consumer from blocking other subscribers.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: One queue consumed by multiple services distributes work rather than delivering an independent copy to each service.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Lambda retry behavior does not replace explicit independent subscription and buffering design.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Network packets are not SNS publish-subscribe delivery semantics.

items.prompt: A notification stream needs ordered messages within each customer and deduplication, and it fans out to FIFO SQS queues. Which SNS topic type should be evaluated?
constraints: Ordering is per customer.
Consumers use FIFO queues.
The producer supplies a stable message identity.

options.text: Evaluate an SNS FIFO topic with message groups and deduplication, then verify that all subscriptions and downstream queues support the required FIFO behavior.
Use an SNS Standard topic because Standard topics always preserve publish order for each subscriber.
Use an S3 event notification because S3 preserves FIFO order when several subscribers receive the same object event.
Use a security group because FIFO topic ordering is enforced by network packet sequence.

feedback.Reason: SNS FIFO topics address ordered and deduplicated publish-subscribe flows when compatible FIFO subscriptions are used.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: SNS FIFO uses message groups and deduplication semantics and can deliver to supported FIFO endpoints. Standard topics do not provide the same ordering guarantee.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner chooses a customer ordering key, configures compatible subscriptions, and tests duplicate publishes and downstream redrive.
Details.errorCorrection: Standard topics do not guarantee the required order, S3 notifications are not FIFO topic delivery, and network sequence is not application ordering.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: FIFO semantics improve correctness but constrain endpoint choices and may trade throughput for ordering guarantees.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Standard SNS topics do not guarantee the required per-customer ordering.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: S3 event notifications do not provide SNS FIFO topic semantics.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Network packet order cannot be used as an application message-ordering guarantee.

items.prompt: An SNS topic carries events for many tenants, but each tenant queue should receive only messages whose tenant attribute matches that queue. Which feature should be used?
constraints: The publisher sets a message attribute.
Consumers need server-side filtering.
The topic remains shared.

options.text: Apply an SNS subscription filter policy on the tenant attribute for each subscription and test behavior when the attribute is missing or malformed.
Publish every message to every queue and filter in consumers because SNS subscription filters cannot inspect message attributes.
Use an SQS visibility timeout because visibility timeout filters messages by tenant before delivery.
Use an IAM group because group membership automatically filters SNS messages by tenant.

feedback.Reason: SNS subscription filter policies can select messages based on message attributes or body according to the configured policy.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Filtering occurs at the subscription, so nonmatching messages are not delivered to that endpoint. Publisher attributes and filter policy behavior must be tested together.
Details.scenarioApplication: The publisher validates tenant attributes, each queue owns its policy, and operations monitors unexpected drops or missing attributes.
Details.errorCorrection: Consumer-side filtering wastes delivery and storage, visibility timeout does not filter content, and IAM groups do not select messages.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Server-side filtering reduces downstream traffic but can silently exclude messages if attribute contracts are not validated.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Consumer filtering delivers unnecessary messages and ignores SNS’s subscription filtering capability.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Visibility timeout controls redelivery timing and does not filter tenant attributes.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: IAM groups authorize identities and do not filter SNS message delivery.

items.prompt: A team subscribes an SQS queue to an SNS topic and messages are not arriving. Which integration dependency should be checked first?
constraints: The queue is in the same or a trusted account.
The topic and queue policies are managed separately.
The subscription must be confirmed and deliverable.

options.text: Verify the SNS subscription exists and is confirmed, the queue policy allows the SNS topic to SendMessage, and the topic and queue are in compatible Regions and accounts.
Grant the consumer role ReceiveMessage only because SNS uses the consumer’s identity to write to the queue.
Make the queue public because SNS cannot publish to a queue protected by a resource policy.
Increase the queue visibility timeout because an unconfirmed subscription hides messages after delivery.

feedback.Reason: SNS-to-SQS delivery depends on a confirmed subscription and an SQS resource policy allowing the SNS service or topic to publish.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: SNS publishes to the queue as a subscription endpoint. The queue policy must authorize the topic, and the subscription must be active before delivery occurs.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner checks confirmation, policy principal and source ARN conditions, and tests a message with delivery metrics and queue depth.
Details.errorCorrection: Consumer ReceiveMessage permission does not authorize SNS to write, public access is unsafe, and visibility timeout applies after receipt.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Resource-policy conditions improve isolation but make topic or account changes a potential delivery failure that needs monitoring.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: The consumer role reads the queue; SNS still needs queue resource authorization to publish.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Public queue access is unnecessary and weakens the delivery boundary.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Visibility timeout cannot fix an unconfirmed subscription or denied SendMessage.

items.prompt: An SNS topic should invoke a Lambda function for each matching notification. What integration permission is required?
constraints: The function is in the same or trusted account.
The topic publishes only approved events.
The function must not be public.

options.text: Create the SNS subscription and grant SNS permission to invoke the Lambda function, scoping the permission to the topic ARN and testing filtered delivery.
Grant the Lambda execution role permission to invoke itself because SNS uses the function’s execution role to call Lambda.
Grant the topic administrator permission to read the function’s environment variables because invocation requires configuration access.
Use a security group because SNS invokes Lambda only when the function and topic share an inbound network rule.

feedback.Reason: SNS needs a resource-based Lambda permission to invoke the function, while the execution role governs what the function does after invocation.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The Lambda function policy authorizes the SNS service and topic as an invocation principal. The function execution role is a separate identity used by the function code.
Details.scenarioApplication: Security scopes the SourceArn, tests approved and denied topics, and makes the handler idempotent for notification retries.
Details.errorCorrection: Self-invocation permissions are not the SNS-to-function permission, environment access is unnecessary, and security groups do not define Lambda invocation.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Resource-based invocation permission is simple but must be reviewed when topics, accounts, or function aliases change.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: The execution role is used by the function and does not grant SNS permission to invoke it.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: SNS does not need to read the function’s environment variables to invoke it.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Lambda invocation authorization is policy based and not controlled by shared security groups.

items.prompt: An HTTPS webhook occasionally returns 503, and the event must be retried before being moved to an operator-managed failure path. Which SNS controls should be evaluated?
constraints: The endpoint can verify SNS messages.
Transient failures may recover.
Permanent failures need isolation.

options.text: Configure the HTTPS subscription delivery retry policy and an SNS subscription DLQ where supported, then make the endpoint idempotent and monitor delivery failures.
Disable retries because an HTTP 503 proves the endpoint permanently rejected the event.
Use an S3 lifecycle rule because lifecycle retries webhook delivery after a failed SNS request.
Use a security group to retry the application request because security groups interpret HTTP status codes.

feedback.Reason: SNS HTTP subscriptions support delivery retries, and a dead-letter path can preserve messages after repeated delivery failure according to the service model.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: SNS retries failed endpoint deliveries using a configured delivery policy and can route undeliverable notifications to a subscription DLQ where supported.
Details.scenarioApplication: The endpoint validates signatures, handles duplicate notifications, and alerts on the DLQ instead of silently losing events.
Details.errorCorrection: A 503 may be transient, S3 lifecycle is unrelated, and security groups do not interpret HTTP responses or schedule retries.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Retries improve delivery but can amplify load during an outage, so backoff, max attempts, and DLQ handling must be explicit.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A 503 can be a transient failure and should not automatically disable recovery attempts.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: S3 lifecycle rules do not retry SNS webhook delivery.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Security groups do not parse HTTP status codes or implement application retries.

items.prompt: An SNS subscription to a Lambda or HTTP endpoint must preserve notifications that cannot be delivered after retries. Which pattern isolates the subscription failures?
constraints: The endpoint can be unavailable for a long period.
Notifications must remain inspectable.
Each subscription has independent failure handling.

options.text: Configure a subscription-level dead-letter queue where supported, grant SNS permission to send there, and monitor and redrive failed notifications only after the endpoint is healthy.
Use the topic’s publish success as proof that every subscriber accepted the message and omit failure storage.
Use one shared queue without subscription context because DLQ messages never need to identify their originating endpoint.
Delete the subscription on the first delivery failure because a DLQ would duplicate the topic message automatically.

feedback.Reason: A subscription DLQ preserves messages that SNS could not deliver to that endpoint after the configured retry policy.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Topic publish acceptance and endpoint delivery are different outcomes. A subscription DLQ has its own queue policy, retention, and redrive process.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner links DLQ messages to the subscription, alerts on age, and replays after fixing the endpoint with idempotent handling.
Details.errorCorrection: Publish success does not prove subscriber delivery, a shared queue can obscure ownership, and deleting a subscription discards the delivery path.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: DLQs improve recovery but add queue cost and replay operations for every independently managed subscription.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: SNS publish success means the topic accepted the message, not that every subscription delivered it.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A shared DLQ without subscription context weakens ownership and replay decisions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Deleting the subscription removes delivery and does not preserve failed notifications.

items.prompt: A webhook endpoint is rate-limited and should receive retries with backoff rather than an immediate retry storm. Which SNS configuration is relevant?
constraints: The endpoint returns transient errors.
The consumer has a known recovery rate.
The publisher should not overwhelm it.

options.text: Configure the SNS delivery policy with an appropriate retry, backoff, and failure boundary, and pair it with endpoint idempotency and monitoring.
Use unlimited immediate retries because retry volume has no effect on the endpoint’s rate limit.
Use SQS visibility timeout because SNS HTTP delivery retries are controlled by the subscriber queue even when no queue exists.
Use Route 53 health checks because health checks set SNS webhook retry intervals and payloads.

feedback.Reason: SNS delivery policies control retry behavior and backoff for supported subscription protocols.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Retry policy parameters determine how SNS responds to failed delivery. Endpoint idempotency is still necessary because a response timeout can make delivery outcome ambiguous.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner models endpoint capacity, configures exponential or linear backoff as appropriate, and sends exhausted failures to a DLQ or alert path.
Details.errorCorrection: Immediate unlimited retries can worsen an outage, SQS visibility applies to queues, and Route 53 health checks do not configure SNS delivery.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Backoff reduces retry storms but extends delivery latency and may require a durable failure path for events beyond the retry window.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Unlimited immediate retries can overload the endpoint and increase the outage.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: SQS visibility timeout is not the retry control for a direct SNS HTTP subscription.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Route 53 health checks do not set SNS retry intervals or message behavior.

items.prompt: Subscribers need to filter events by event type, tenant, and priority without parsing the full message body. Which publisher behavior is required?
constraints: The filter policy uses message attributes.
Publishers are centrally governed.
Missing attributes must be treated deliberately.

options.text: Publish validated message attributes with stable names and types, document their contract, and test filter behavior for matching, nonmatching, and missing attributes.
Put attributes in an undocumented string because SNS converts any string into a typed filter value automatically.
Omit attributes and filter only by security-group membership because subscriber networks define event type.
Use a KMS key alias as the event priority because key names are delivered as SNS message attributes by default.

feedback.Reason: SNS filter policies depend on message attributes or body structure that publishers must provide consistently.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Attribute names, data types, and policy operators determine whether a subscription receives a message. Missing or malformed attributes can cause unintended filtering.
Details.scenarioApplication: The event schema validates attributes before publish and includes test cases for every subscription policy.
Details.errorCorrection: Undocumented strings do not guarantee typed filtering, network membership is unrelated, and KMS aliases are not message attributes.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Attribute filtering reduces consumer work but couples publishers and subscriptions to a shared event contract.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Filtering depends on the configured attribute type and policy behavior; undocumented strings are not a safe contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Network placement does not define event type or subscription filtering.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: KMS aliases are not automatically published as SNS message attributes.

items.prompt: An SQS consumer expects the exact published JSON body and should not parse the default SNS envelope. Which subscription setting should be evaluated?
constraints: The consumer owns the event schema.
The topic may have mixed subscription types.
Envelope metadata is not required by this consumer.

options.text: Enable raw message delivery for that compatible subscription and verify that the consumer still receives the attributes and metadata it needs through the supported format.
Strip the envelope in the SQS consumer without checking the subscription setting because SNS never wraps messages for queues.
Use a security group because raw delivery is a network transformation applied to queue packets.
Use S3 object metadata because SNS raw delivery is controlled by bucket object headers.

feedback.Reason: SNS raw message delivery changes the subscription payload shape for supported endpoints and must match consumer expectations.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: By default, SNS can deliver a message envelope. Raw delivery removes that envelope for a subscription, so consumers and message-attribute handling must be tested.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner enables it only for consumers with the exact contract and keeps other subscribers on the envelope when they need topic metadata.
Details.errorCorrection: Queues can receive SNS envelopes, security groups do not transform payloads, and S3 metadata is unrelated.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Raw delivery simplifies consumers but can remove metadata they relied on, so schema compatibility is the deciding factor.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: SNS subscription configuration determines whether the envelope is present; consumer stripping is not the only option.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Raw delivery is a service payload setting, not a network transformation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: S3 object metadata does not control SNS subscription payloads.

items.prompt: An SNS topic carries confidential notifications and must use a customer managed KMS key with separate publisher and subscriber roles. Which design dependency matters?
constraints: The topic uses server-side encryption.
The key is customer managed.
Workloads must not administer the key.

options.text: Configure SNS server-side encryption with the selected KMS key, align key and IAM policies for the SNS service and required publishers or consumers, and test key rotation or denial behavior.
Grant kms:* to every subscriber because encrypted SNS delivery cannot work with resource-scoped key permissions.
Use a security group for the key because topic encryption is controlled by the publisher subnet.
Use TLS only because encryption in transit automatically gives the topic customer-managed at-rest encryption.

feedback.Reason: SNS server-side encryption adds KMS policy dependencies that must be scoped and tested separately from transport TLS.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: SNS uses the configured KMS key for topic message encryption at rest. Key policies, IAM permissions, grants, and service behavior must permit required publish or delivery operations.
Details.scenarioApplication: Security grants only required key actions, tests publishing and subscription delivery, and plans key lifecycle without deleting a key still needed by retained messages.
Details.errorCorrection: Scoped permissions are supported, security groups do not authorize KMS, and TLS does not replace at-rest encryption with the customer key.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Customer keys improve ownership and auditability but add policy and availability dependencies to the publish path.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Workloads should not receive unrestricted key administration merely because the topic is encrypted.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: KMS key authorization is policy based and not controlled by security groups.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: TLS protects network transport and does not meet the customer-managed at-rest requirement.

items.prompt: A producer in Account A must publish to an SNS topic owned by Account B, but it must not subscribe or administer the topic. Which authorization is appropriate?
constraints: The topic owner controls the resource policy.
The producer role is known.
Publish is the only required action.

options.text: Allow the producer principal to sns:Publish in the topic resource policy and its identity policy, scoped to the topic ARN, while keeping subscribe and administration actions separate.
Grant sns:* to the producer account because cross-account SNS requires every action to be allowed.
Make the topic public because a resource policy cannot name a principal from another account.
Use VPC peering because private network connectivity grants cross-account SNS publish access.

feedback.Reason: Cross-account SNS publishing requires compatible identity and topic resource policies, and the producer should receive only publish permission.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The topic owner’s resource policy can trust a principal from another account, while the caller’s identity policy must also permit Publish. Resource policies do not automatically grant administration.
Details.scenarioApplication: Security tests publish and denied subscribe or delete operations and conditions the policy on the exact topic ARN and principal.
Details.errorCorrection: sns:* is excessive, public access is unsafe, and VPC peering does not grant service API authorization.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Cross-account policies support central event ownership but require lifecycle review when producer accounts or roles change.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: The producer needs only Publish, not every SNS action.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A public topic weakens the trust boundary and is not required for cross-account publishing.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Network connectivity does not authorize SNS API operations.

items.prompt: A producer retries publishing an order event after a timeout and must avoid duplicate publication within the FIFO deduplication interval. Which value should remain stable?
constraints: The order event has a durable identifier.
The producer may retry.
Subscribers still handle duplicate side effects defensively.

options.text: Reuse a stable MessageDeduplicationId for the same logical event or use supported content-based deduplication, and keep subscribers idempotent.
Generate a random deduplication ID for every retry so SNS can correlate retries by their different values.
Use a new topic for each retry because SNS deduplicates only when topics have unique names.
Disable retry because a timed-out publish is guaranteed not to have reached SNS.

feedback.Reason: SNS FIFO deduplication requires the same identity for repeated publication of one logical message.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: FIFO topics use MessageDeduplicationId or content-based deduplication within a bounded interval. A publish timeout leaves the outcome ambiguous.
Details.scenarioApplication: The producer persists the event ID, reuses it on retry, and the consumer protects external side effects beyond the deduplication window.
Details.errorCorrection: Random IDs defeat deduplication, topic names do not correlate messages, and disabling retries can lose a valid event.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Topic deduplication reduces duplicate deliveries within its window but is not an end-to-end transaction or idempotency store.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Different IDs tell SNS that retry messages are distinct.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Creating topics per retry is not the FIFO deduplication mechanism.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A timeout does not prove that SNS rejected the publish.

items.prompt: Events for each warehouse must preserve order, but independent warehouses should be published and consumed concurrently through SNS FIFO and SQS FIFO. Which key should define the group?
constraints: Order is required per warehouse.
Warehouses are independent.
The group key is stable for the event sequence.

options.text: Use the warehouse identifier as the MessageGroupId so each warehouse has an ordered sequence while different warehouses can progress in parallel.
Use one global group ID because FIFO parallelism increases when every message shares a group.
Use a random group ID for every message because FIFO will reconstruct warehouse order from timestamps.
Use an S3 prefix because SNS FIFO reads message-group order from object key paths.

feedback.Reason: SNS FIFO message groups establish the ordering boundary and should map to the business entity whose events must remain ordered.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Messages with the same group ID are ordered; different groups can be processed concurrently by compatible FIFO subscribers.
Details.scenarioApplication: The publisher uses the warehouse key, monitors a hot warehouse group, and keeps event IDs stable for deduplication.
Details.errorCorrection: One global group serializes all warehouses, random IDs destroy the ordering boundary, and S3 prefixes are unrelated.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Business-key grouping improves concurrency but can create a hot group if one entity dominates traffic.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: One group creates one serialization boundary and reduces concurrency.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Random groups cannot preserve per-warehouse order.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: SNS FIFO groups are message properties, not S3 object prefixes.

items.prompt: A product needs one service to send notifications to mobile devices across supported platform push services, while device tokens and endpoint status are managed centrally. Which capability should be evaluated?
constraints: The destination is mobile push endpoints.
The service needs platform-specific credential integration.
Invalid endpoints require lifecycle handling.

options.text: Evaluate Amazon SNS mobile push with platform applications and device endpoints, and design token refresh, endpoint disablement, payload, and delivery failure handling.
Use SQS because SQS automatically translates one message into native Apple and Android push notifications.
Use a VPC endpoint because mobile push delivery is an internal subnet broadcast to device IP addresses.
Use S3 event notifications because object events automatically maintain device endpoint registrations.

feedback.Reason: SNS mobile push is the service capability for publishing notifications to platform endpoints through configured mobile applications.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: SNS manages platform application and endpoint resources, but the application must handle device-token changes, invalid endpoints, payload rules, and delivery outcomes.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner registers platform credentials, updates endpoint tokens, disables invalid endpoints, and monitors delivery failures.
Details.errorCorrection: SQS is a queue and does not translate to mobile push protocols, VPC endpoints are network paths, and S3 events do not manage device tokens.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Centralized push delivery reduces platform-specific integration work but introduces token lifecycle and notification delivery governance.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: SQS provides queue delivery and does not natively translate messages to mobile push endpoints.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Mobile push is not a VPC subnet broadcast or private endpoint operation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: S3 event notifications do not register or manage mobile device endpoints.

items.prompt: An event payload exceeds the SNS message size limit, but subscribers should still receive a durable reference and verify access. Which pattern should be used?
constraints: The payload is stored securely.
Subscribers can read the referenced object.
The event must remain meaningful if the object expires.

options.text: Store the large payload in an access-controlled S3 object and publish a compact SNS event containing a validated pointer, checksum or version, and retention contract.
Split the payload into unrelated SNS messages because subscribers can always reconstruct order without a correlation identifier.
Make the S3 object public because SNS subscribers cannot use resource policies to read a private payload.
Use a KMS alias as the payload because key names can contain unlimited message bytes and are delivered to subscribers.

feedback.Reason: A pointer pattern keeps SNS messages within limits while preserving secure, versioned access to the large payload.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The event carries metadata and a reference; the subscriber uses its own authorization to retrieve the object. Object version, checksum, and retention prevent ambiguous or missing payloads.
Details.scenarioApplication: The producer writes the object before publishing, and consumers handle missing, unauthorized, or expired references explicitly.
Details.errorCorrection: Uncorrelated chunks can be reordered or lost, public objects weaken confidentiality, and KMS aliases are not payload storage.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Pointer-based delivery adds a second read and lifecycle dependency but avoids oversized messages and supports independent payload retention.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Chunking needs explicit correlation and ordering and can create a fragile multi-message protocol.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Subscribers can be authorized through S3 policies; public exposure is unnecessary.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: KMS aliases identify keys and cannot contain the event payload.

items.prompt: A batch job should publish only approved event types to one topic and must not subscribe, delete, or modify the topic. Which permission shape is correct?
constraints: The producer role is dedicated.
The topic ARN is known.
Administrative actions are separate.

options.text: Grant the producer role sns:Publish only on the specific topic ARN, use message-schema validation in the application, and keep topic administration and subscription permissions separate.
Grant sns:* because a publisher cannot work unless it can administer every topic property.
Use a security group because it can distinguish event types and prevent the role from modifying a topic policy.
Use an API key without an IAM or resource policy because SNS publish authorization is optional for private workloads.

feedback.Reason: The producer needs a narrowly scoped Publish action; message content validation and topic administration are separate controls.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: IAM identity and topic resource policies authorize sns:Publish. They do not validate arbitrary event semantics, which belongs in the producer contract or schema.
Details.scenarioApplication: Security tests publish to the intended topic and denies Subscribe, DeleteTopic, and SetTopicAttributes from the producer.
Details.errorCorrection: sns:* expands blast radius, security groups do not protect topic policies, and private workloads still require authorization.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Least privilege reduces compromise impact but requires updating policy when topic ownership or event routing changes.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Publishers do not need topic administration or subscription-management actions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Security groups are network controls and do not authorize SNS actions or message types.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: SNS API operations remain authorized by policies regardless of workload network placement.

items.prompt: A subscriber must absorb a three-hour outage and process notifications later without losing them. Why is a direct SNS-to-HTTP subscription insufficient by itself?
constraints: The subscriber is unavailable during the outage.
Events must be buffered durably.
Processing can resume after recovery.

options.text: Subscribe an SQS queue to the SNS topic and have the service process the queue after recovery, using retry, retention, DLQ, and idempotency controls.
Use a direct SNS HTTP subscription only because SNS retains every notification indefinitely for an unavailable endpoint.
Use a security group to buffer notifications because blocked HTTP traffic is stored by the network until the endpoint recovers.
Use a Route 53 record because DNS failover stores undelivered notifications for the subscriber.

feedback.Reason: SQS provides durable buffering and consumer-controlled retry; direct SNS delivery is not an indefinite outage buffer.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: SNS delivers to a subscription according to its retry and failure policy. An SQS subscription stores the copy until a consumer receives and deletes it, subject to retention.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner sets queue retention beyond the outage, configures a DLQ, and scales the consumer gradually after recovery.
Details.errorCorrection: Direct HTTP delivery can exhaust retries, security groups do not buffer application messages, and DNS does not store events.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Adding SQS costs and operational components but decouples subscriber availability from publisher delivery.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Direct SNS delivery has a configured retry and failure behavior and does not retain every notification indefinitely.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Network blocking drops or rejects traffic; it is not a durable message buffer.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DNS failover changes name resolution and does not store undelivered notifications.
